adept.definition: highly skilled and proficient at something
sentences: Although she had never sailed before, the young diplomat proved adept at navigating the delicate negotiations between the two rival delegations.
Years of practice made the old carpenter so adept with his tools that he could craft a flawless drawer in an afternoon.
adept.mnemonic: Adept ≠ adepte (disciple) : l'adept est surtout doué, pas fidèle.

advocate.definition: to publicly support or recommend a cause or policy
sentences: The senator has long advocated stricter environmental regulations, arguing that voluntary measures by industry have repeatedly failed to protect the nation's rivers.
Many economists advocate lowering trade barriers, convinced that open markets ultimately benefit consumers even if some domestic producers suffer in the short term.
advocate.mnemonic: Un avocat plaide, mais to advocate = prôner une cause, pas exercer la profession.

affluent.definition: having a great deal of money; wealthy
sentences: The affluent suburb, with its sprawling lawns and gated mansions, stood in sharp contrast to the struggling neighborhoods just across the highway.
Because the region had become increasingly affluent, restaurants and boutiques catering to wealthy residents multiplied rapidly along the once-quiet main street.
The photographer's most arresting image showed a lone fisherman silhouetted against a blood-red sky, and visitors paused before it for several minutes.
Critics praised the novel's arresting opening line, which was so startling that readers felt compelled to continue past the first page.
arresting.mnemonic: Une image « arrête » le regard : elle vous saisit.

candid.definition: honest and straightforward, even when the truth is uncomfortable
sentences: In a candid interview, the retiring coach admitted that the team's poor season resulted from his own strategic mistakes rather than from bad luck.
Her candid assessment of the manuscript, though painful for the author to hear, was exactly the honest feedback needed to improve the book.
candid.mnemonic: Candid ≠ candide : en anglais, franc ; en français, naïf.

catholic.definition: broad and wide-ranging, especially in interests or tastes
sentences: The librarian's catholic taste in reading ranged from medieval poetry and quantum physics to detective fiction and obscure cookbooks.
Unlike colleagues who studied only one narrow period, the historian had catholic interests that embraced almost every era and region of the world.
catholic.mnemonic: Catholique vient du grec « universel » : catholic = très large.

censure.definition: to criticize or condemn formally and severely
sentences: The committee voted to censure the mayor for misusing public funds, though it stopped short of demanding that he resign from office.
Parliament moved to censure the minister after he misled lawmakers, publicly condemning his conduct as a serious breach of the trust of voters.
censure.mnemonic: Censure anglaise = blâme officiel, pas interdiction d'un contenu.

chauvinism.definition: prejudiced belief in the superiority of one's own sex or group
sentences: The executive's open chauvinism, which led him to ignore every suggestion made by his female colleagues, eventually prompted a formal complaint to human resources.
Feminist writers of the 1970s exposed the male chauvinism embedded in everyday language, advertising, and hiring practices, which had long been dismissed as harmless tradition.
chauvinism.mnemonic: Chauvinisme patriotique en français ; au GRE, souvent « male chauvinism ».

complacent.definition: smugly self-satisfied and unaware of possible dangers or the need to improve
sentences: After three consecutive championships, the team grew complacent, skipping practices and assuming that victory would come automatically, and a humiliating defeat soon followed.
Health officials warned that the public must not become complacent about the virus, since relaxed precautions could quickly allow infections to surge again.
complacent.mnemonic: Complacent ≠ complaisant : trop content de soi, donc endormi.

condone.definition: to overlook or tolerate wrongdoing, treating it as acceptable
sentences: The principal refused to condone cheating, insisting that any student caught copying answers would face suspension regardless of past academic performance.
By failing to punish the offenders, the board seemed to condone the harassment, and critics accused its members of quietly tolerating abuse.
condone.mnemonic: Condone ≠ condamner : c'est exactement le contraire !

contention.definition: a claim or argument asserted in a debate
sentences: The biologist's central contention, that the species evolved far earlier than previously believed, was challenged by several skeptical colleagues at the conference.
Her contention that the policy would reduce unemployment was undermined by the data, which showed that joblessness had actually risen since its introduction.
contention.mnemonic: Contention ≠ contention médicale : ici, thèse défendue ou querelle.

destitute.definition: lacking the basic necessities of life; extremely poor
sentences: After the factory closed and the family lost their home, they were left destitute, dependent on charity for food and shelter.
The novelist depicted the destitute orphans of the industrial city, children so poor that they scavenged scraps of bread from the gutters.
destitute.mnemonic: Destitué = démis ; destitute = dépourvu de tout, sans un sou.

disinterested.definition: impartial; free from personal bias or self-interest
sentences: A judge must remain disinterested in the outcome of a trial, ruling solely on the evidence rather than on any personal gain.
Seeking a disinterested opinion, the company hired an outside auditor with no financial stake in the results to review the disputed accounts.
disinterested.mnemonic: Disinterested = impartial ; ne pas confondre avec uninterested (indifférent).

enervate.definition: to weaken or drain of energy and vitality
sentences: The oppressive tropical heat seemed to enervate the expedition members, who dragged themselves forward with barely enough strength to lift their packs.
Critics argued that years of constant fighting would enervate the nation, draining its resources and leaving its citizens too exhausted to rebuild.
enervate.mnemonic: Enervate ≠ énerver : il ne rend pas nerveux, il affaiblit.

exigent.definition: urgent and demanding immediate attention or action
sentences: The hospital's exigent need for blood donors, caused by a sudden highway accident, led administrators to broadcast an emergency appeal across the region.
Faced with exigent circumstances, the captain abandoned his careful plans and ordered the crew to patch the hull at once before the ship sank.
exigent.mnemonic: Exigent ≠ exigeant : ce sont les circonstances qui sont pressantes.

expeditious.definition: quick and efficient, done with speed and skill
sentences: The clerk's expeditious handling of the paperwork meant that applicants received their permits within a day instead of waiting several weeks.
Praising the engineers for their expeditious repair of the bridge, the governor noted that traffic resumed far sooner than anyone had predicted.
expeditious.mnemonic: Expeditious ≠ expéditif : vite ET bien fait, sens positif.

fastidious.definition: very attentive to detail and hard to please
sentences: The fastidious editor combed through every paragraph, correcting even the smallest errors in punctuation before allowing the book to go to press.
Known for his fastidious habits, the chef insisted that every knife be polished and every ingredient measured precisely before service began.

fitness.definition: suitability or qualification for a particular purpose or role
sentences: The committee questioned the nominee's fitness for the judgeship, citing her lack of experience and several controversial rulings earlier in her career.
Darwin argued that an organism's evolutionary fitness depends on how well its traits suit its environment, not on its strength alone.
fitness.mnemonic: Fitness = adéquation (« fit for the job »), pas seulement le sport.

formidable.definition: inspiring fear or awe because of size, power, or difficulty
sentences: The challenger faced a formidable opponent, a champion who had never lost a match and whose sheer power intimidated even veteran players.
Scaling the icy north face proved a formidable task, so daunting that most of the climbers privately doubted they would succeed.
formidable.mnemonic: Formidable en anglais fait peur : il ne veut pas dire « génial ».

sentences: A fortuitous meeting with a publisher on the train led the unknown author to a lucrative contract she had never expected.
The discovery of penicillin is often called fortuitous, since the mold that spoiled Fleming's experiment happened by luck to produce a life-saving drug.
fortuitous.mnemonic: Fortuitous contient « fortune » : un hasard heureux.

futile.definition: pointless; incapable of producing any useful result
sentences: Rescuers realized that further digging was futile, since the collapsed mine had been sealed for days and no one could have survived.
Arguing with the committee proved futile; despite hours of eloquent protest, the members refused to reconsider their decision.
futile.mnemonic: Futile ≠ futile (frivole) : en anglais, inutile, voué à l'échec.

gauche.definition: socially awkward, lacking tact or polish
sentences: The teenager's gauche attempt at small talk, in which he loudly asked the ambassador how much his watch cost, left the guests cringing.
Although brilliant in the laboratory, the young scientist was gauche at formal dinners and often committed embarrassing blunders in front of influential donors.
gauche.mnemonic: Gauche = côté gauche, maladroit : « avoir deux mains gauches ».

hardy.definition: robust and able to endure difficult conditions
sentences: Only the hardy mountain goats could survive the brutal winters on the exposed ridge, where temperatures dropped far below freezing.
The gardener chose hardy perennials that would withstand frost and drought, since she rarely had time to protect the flowers.

incense.definition: to make extremely angry; to enrage
sentences: The company's decision to lay off hundreds of workers while paying executives huge bonuses incensed the community and sparked angry protests outside headquarters.
Nothing could incense the old professor more than students who plagiarized, and he would turn red with fury whenever he discovered copied passages.
incense.mnemonic: Incense verbe = mettre en fureur, pas l'encens (qui est un nom : incense).

inconsequential.definition: of little or no importance or significance
sentences: The mayor dismissed the complaints as inconsequential, insisting that the minor delays would have no effect on the project's overall success.
What seemed an inconsequential remark at the dinner party later proved crucial, for it revealed the secret that the detective had been seeking.
inconsequential.mnemonic: Inconsequential ≠ inconséquent : sans conséquence, donc sans importance.

sentences: The inept waiter spilled soup on two customers and then forgot the third table's order entirely, prompting the manager to apologize profusely.
Critics blamed the crisis on the government's inept handling of the economy, pointing to a series of blunders that showed its lack of competence.

ingenuous.definition: innocent and trusting; lacking worldly cunning
sentences: The ingenuous young tourist trusted every stranger who offered help, never suspecting that some of them intended to cheat him.
Her ingenuous questions about politics, asked with complete sincerity and no hidden agenda, charmed the senator and disarmed his usual defensiveness.
ingenuous.mnemonic: Ingenuous ≠ ingenious (ingénieux) : ingénu, naïf et sincère.

integral.definition: essential and necessary to make something complete
sentences: Music is an integral part of the festival, so organizers refused to cut the orchestra even when the budget shrank dramatically.
The treaty's final clause, once viewed as a minor detail, proved integral to the agreement, because without it neither side would have signed.
integral.mnemonic: Integral = partie intégrante : on ne peut pas l'enlever.

martinet.definition: a person who enforces strict discipline and rigid obedience to rules
martinet.definitionFr: personne qui impose une discipline de fer
sentences: The new sergeant was a notorious martinet, inspecting every bunk with white gloves and punishing recruits for the slightest wrinkle in a blanket.
Employees dreaded working for the office martinet, who timed their lunch breaks to the second and reprimanded anyone who arrived a minute late.
martinet.mnemonic: Le martinet (fouet) = image du chef qui fouette la discipline.

mercurial.definition: unpredictable and prone to sudden changes of mood
sentences: The director's mercurial temperament made rehearsals unpredictable, for he could shift from joyful praise to furious shouting within a single minute.
Investors grew wary of the mercurial founder, whose enthusiasm for new projects changed so quickly that no strategy ever lasted through a single quarter.
mercurial.mnemonic: Mercure, le métal liquide et vif : humeur qui change sans cesse.

sentences: The detective examined the minute traces of blood on the floor, each smaller than a grain of sand, through a powerful magnifying glass.
Even a minute error in the calculation could cause the spacecraft to miss its target by thousands of miles, so engineers checked every figure.
minute.mnemonic: Minute adjectif se prononce maï-nioute : minuscule, pas la durée.

miscreant.definition: a person who behaves badly or breaks the law; a wrongdoer
sentences: The village constable chased the miscreant who had been vandalizing shop windows at night, and soon brought the young troublemaker before the magistrate.
Once a respected banker, he was now branded a miscreant by the press after investigators uncovered his scheme to defraud thousands of elderly clients.
miscreant.mnemonic: Miscreant ≠ mécréant (incroyant) : un voyou, pas un athée.

miser.definition: a person who hoards money and spends as little as possible
sentences: The old miser refused to heat his house in winter, counting every coin in his cellar while his neighbors wondered at his poverty-like habits.
Dickens's Scrooge is the classic miser, a man so devoted to hoarding wealth that he begrudges his clerk a single lump of coal.
miser.mnemonic: Miser rime avec misère : il vit pauvre alors qu'il est riche.

motif.definition: a recurring theme, subject, or distinctive idea in a work of art
sentences: The recurring motif of water in the novel, appearing in storms, rivers, and tears, symbolizes the characters' longing for renewal.
Throughout the symphony, a haunting four-note motif returns in different keys, tying the separate movements together into one unified work.
motif.mnemonic: Motif ≠ raison : en anglais, thème récurrent d'une œuvre.

mundane.definition: ordinary, dull, and concerned with everyday matters
sentences: After the thrill of the expedition, the explorer found the mundane routines of office life, with its meetings and memos, almost unbearable.
The poet had a gift for finding beauty in mundane objects, transforming a chipped teacup or a worn doorstep into subjects of wonder.
mundane.mnemonic: Mundane ≠ mondain : du monde quotidien, pas de la haute société.

sentences: The magician's final trick continued to mystify the audience, who could find no explanation for how the elephant had vanished from the stage.
Scientists remain mystified by the strange signal from deep space, which follows a pattern that none of their existing theories can account for.
mystify.mnemonic: Mystify ≠ mystifier : ici on désoriente, on ne dupe pas.

noisome.definition: having an extremely offensive or foul smell; disgusting
sentences: The noisome stench rising from the abandoned sewer forced the workers to cover their faces and retreat before they could finish the inspection.
Residents complained about the noisome fumes drifting from the chemical plant, a repulsive odor so strong that it made schoolchildren feel sick.
noisome.mnemonic: Noisome n'a rien à voir avec noisy : ça sent mauvais, ça ne fait pas de bruit.

notorious.definition: famous or well known for something bad
sentences: The notorious bandit, wanted in three states for robbing stagecoaches, was finally captured after a decade of eluding the sheriff.
The city became notorious for its corrupt police force, a bad reputation that discouraged tourists and investors from coming to the region.
notorious.mnemonic: Notorious ≠ notoire : toujours en mal, jamais en bien.

novel.definition: new, original, and unlike anything previously known
sentences: The young engineer proposed a novel approach to desalination, one that differed so radically from existing methods that experts were initially skeptical.
Because the technique was entirely novel, no textbook described it, and surgeons had to learn the procedure directly from its inventor.
novel.mnemonic: Novel adjectif = nouveau (nova), pas un roman.

officious.definition: intrusively eager to offer unwanted help or advice
sentences: The officious clerk kept hovering over customers, offering unwanted advice and rearranging their purchases until they politely begged him to leave them alone.
Her officious neighbor constantly interfered in the family's affairs, offering opinions on their parenting and garden that nobody had requested.
officious.mnemonic: Officious ≠ officieux : trop zélé, il se mêle de tout.

onerous.definition: burdensome; requiring great effort or involving heavy obligations
sentences: The new regulations imposed such onerous paperwork on small businesses that many owners hired extra staff just to keep up with the demands.
Caring for three aging relatives was an onerous duty, one that left her exhausted and with almost no time for her own life.
onerous.mnemonic: Onerous ≠ onéreux (coûteux) : c'est la charge qui pèse, pas le prix.

patent.definition: obvious and plain to see; clearly evident
sentences: It was patent to everyone in the room that the witness was lying, for his story contradicted itself within a few sentences.
The senator's patent disregard for the facts, obvious even to his supporters, damaged his credibility more than any rival's attack could have.
patent.mnemonic: Patent = « patent » = ouvert à tous les yeux : évident.

pedestrian.definition: dull and unimaginative; ordinary and lacking inspiration
sentences: Reviewers dismissed the film as pedestrian, noting that its predictable plot and flat dialogue offered nothing that audiences had not already seen many times.
Although technically correct, the student's essay was pedestrian, lacking the spark of original thought that would have distinguished it from the other submissions.
pedestrian.mnemonic: Le piéton marche à pied, terre à terre : style plat, sans éclat.

petulant.definition: childishly sulky and irritable when not getting one's way
sentences: When the referee overturned his goal, the star striker threw a petulant tantrum, kicking the ball into the stands and sulking on the bench.
The petulant child folded her arms and refused to eat, complaining loudly that nobody had asked her what she wanted for dinner.
petulant.mnemonic: Petulant ≠ pétulant (plein d'entrain) : ici, il boude comme un enfant.

plastic.definition: easily shaped or molded; capable of being changed
sentences: The sculptor preferred wet clay because its plastic quality allowed her to reshape the figure repeatedly until she achieved the form she wanted.
Neuroscientists describe the young brain as remarkably plastic, able to rewire itself in response to new experiences far more easily than an adult's.
plastic.mnemonic: Plastic ici = modelable (du grec plassein, former), pas la matière.

prevaricate.definition: to speak evasively in order to avoid telling the truth
prevaricate.definitionFr: éluder la vérité, noyer le poisson
sentences: Rather than admit that the funds were missing, the treasurer chose to prevaricate, answering each pointed question with vague and rambling remarks.
Pressed by reporters about the scandal, the spokesman continued to prevaricate, offering evasive replies that avoided any direct statement of the facts.
prevaricate.mnemonic: Prevaricate ≠ prévariquer : on tourne autour du pot, on n'est pas corrompu.

prominent.definition: important, well known, or standing out in a position of note
prominent.definitionFr: en vue, important, de premier plan
sentences: As a prominent surgeon and former head of the medical association, she was frequently consulted by journalists on questions of national health policy.
The company's founder played a prominent role in the town's affairs, funding the library and serving on nearly every important civic committee.
prominent.mnemonic: Prominent ≠ proéminent (physique) : ici, de premier plan.

propriety.definition: conformity to accepted standards of proper behavior and manners
sentences: Victorian society placed enormous value on propriety, expecting young women to follow strict rules about how they dressed, spoke, and conducted themselves.
Offended by the senator's crude jokes, the audience felt he had violated all sense of propriety expected of a public official at such a ceremony.
propriety.mnemonic: Propriety ≠ propriété : les convenances, ce qui est « proper ».

prowess.definition: exceptional skill or ability in a particular activity
sentences: The young pianist's technical prowess astonished the judges, who agreed that no competitor had ever played such difficult passages with such ease.
Admired for his military prowess, the general won battle after battle, and his skill in strategy became legendary throughout the empire.
prowess.mnemonic: Prowess : la prouesse, mais au sens de compétence habituelle.

rapport.definition: a harmonious relationship marked by mutual understanding and sympathy
sentences: The therapist worked hard to build rapport with her patients, knowing that trust and mutual understanding were essential before any real progress could begin.
A natural rapport developed between the two negotiators, who quickly found common ground and began to joke easily despite representing opposing sides.
rapport.mnemonic: Rapport ≠ rapport écrit : ici, une bonne entente, une complicité.

rebut.definition: to disprove or argue against a claim with evidence
sentences: In her closing statement, the defense attorney sought to rebut each of the prosecutor's claims by presenting documents that proved her client's innocence.
The scientist published a detailed paper to rebut critics who had questioned her data, offering new experiments that directly disproved their objections.
rebut.mnemonic: Rebut ≠ rebut (déchet) : ici on réfute un argument.

refrain.definition: to hold oneself back from doing something
sentences: Visitors to the museum are asked to refrain from using flash photography, since the bright light can damage the fragile paintings.
Although he was tempted to retort angrily, the diplomat chose to refrain from replying, knowing that silence would better protect the delicate talks.
refrain.mnemonic: Refrain verbe = se retenir (« refrain from »), pas le refrain d'une chanson.

restive.definition: restless and unable to stay still or be controlled
restive.definitionFr: agité, incapable de tenir en place
sentences: As the lecture dragged into its third hour, the restive audience began shifting in their seats and glancing impatiently at their watches.
The restive horse pawed the ground and tossed its head, refusing to stand still while the rider tried to mount it.
restive.mnemonic: Restive ≠ rester : au contraire, il ne peut pas rester en place.

sanction.definition: to give official permission or approval for something
sentences: The university refused to sanction the protest, insisting that students needed official permission before holding any demonstration on the campus grounds.
Only the governor had the authority to sanction the new highway, and she approved the plan after months of study and public hearings.
sanction.mnemonic: Sanction verbe = approuver (sens rare) ; attention, pas punir ici.

sanguine.definition: optimistic and confident, especially in a difficult situation
sentences: Despite three consecutive failed experiments, the sanguine researcher remained confident that a breakthrough was only weeks away and encouraged her discouraged team.
Analysts were sanguine about the economy's prospects, predicting that growth would recover soon even though recent figures had been disappointing.
sanguine.mnemonic: Sanguine ≠ sanguin (colérique) : le sang chaud rend optimiste, pas furieux.

solicitous.definition: showing attentive care and concern for someone's well-being
sentences: The solicitous nurse checked on the elderly patient every hour, adjusting his pillows and asking whether he needed water or another blanket.
Her solicitous host hovered around the guests, constantly refilling glasses and inquiring whether everyone was comfortable and enjoying the meal.
solicitous.mnemonic: Solicitous ≠ soucieux (inquiet) : attentionné, aux petits soins.

solvent.definition: having enough money to pay all one's debts
solvent.definitionFr: solvable, capable de payer ses dettes
sentences: Despite the recession, the family business remained solvent, with enough cash in reserve to pay all its suppliers and employees on time.
Auditors confirmed that the bank was still solvent, meaning its assets exceeded its debts, and they urged depositors not to panic.
solvent.mnemonic: Solvent adjectif ≠ solvant chimique : il peut payer ses dettes.

suppress.definition: to forcibly put an end to or hold back something
sentences: The regime used troops to suppress the uprising, arresting its leaders and crushing every attempt at open resistance across the northern provinces.
Officials tried to suppress the report, hoping that hiding its damaging findings would prevent a public scandal before the election.
suppress.mnemonic: Suppress ≠ supprimer (effacer) : on étouffe, on écrase.

susceptible.definition: likely to be affected by something; vulnerable
sentences: Elderly patients are especially susceptible to pneumonia, so doctors recommend that they receive vaccinations before the cold season begins.
Because he was so susceptible to flattery, the king was easily manipulated by advisors who praised every one of his decisions.
susceptible.mnemonic: Susceptible ≠ susceptible (vexable) : exposé à un danger ou une influence.

testament.definition: clear proof or evidence of something's existence or value
sentences: The cathedral's soaring spires stand as a testament to the skill and devotion of the medieval craftsmen who built it.
Her recovery after the accident was a testament to her courage, offering clear evidence of the extraordinary determination she possessed.
testament.mnemonic: Testament = « testimony » : preuve, pas seulement le testament d'héritage.

titular.definition: holding a title or office in name only, without real power
titular.definitionFr: de nom seulement, sans pouvoir réel
sentences: The queen was merely the titular head of state, since real power lay with the elected parliament and its prime minister.
Although he was the company's titular chairman, he rarely attended meetings, leaving every important decision to the executives who actually ran the firm.
titular.mnemonic: Titular ≠ titulaire : il porte le titre mais n'a pas le pouvoir.

treatise.definition: a formal, systematic written work on a particular subject
sentences: Adam Smith's lengthy treatise on economics, published in 1776, systematically examined how wealth is created and distributed across a nation.
The philosopher spent a decade writing a treatise on ethics, a dense scholarly work that scholars still study in universities today.
treatise.mnemonic: Treatise ≠ treaty : l'un est un livre, l'autre un accord.

truculent.definition: eager to fight; aggressively defiant and hostile
sentences: The truculent customer slammed his fist on the counter and shouted threats at the staff, apparently eager to start a fight.
Truculent and defiant, the prisoner glared at his guards and answered every question with an insult, refusing to cooperate in any way.
truculent.mnemonic: Truculent ≠ truculent (haut en couleur) : en anglais, il cherche la bagarre.

urbane.definition: polite, refined, and confident in social situations
urbane.definitionFr: courtois, policé, à l'aise en société
sentences: The urbane ambassador charmed the guests with witty conversation and impeccable manners, putting even the most nervous visitors at ease.
With his urbane charm and polished manners, the diplomat handled the awkward dinner gracefully, smoothing over every tense moment.
urbane.mnemonic: Urbane ≠ urbain (de la ville) : poli et raffiné, comme un citadin.
